title: Linux, Networking, and Cloud Systems Engineering
centralQuestion: What actually happens beneath containers, Kubernetes, and cloud abstractions, and how can a host be operated from evidence rather than guesswork?
responsibility: Build and operate a production-shaped Linux host with explicit process, identity, resource, storage, network, trust, virtualization, cloud, and recovery boundaries.
incomingBoundary: Basic programming, basic command-line use, and no assumed Linux administration, networking, or cloud experience.
outgoingBoundary: Atlas Host Runtime 1.0 plus exact compute, identity, network, storage, DNS, load-balancing, metadata, observability, recovery, and failure-domain requirements ready for Course 2 infrastructure-as-code implementation.
versionState: Atlas Host Runtime Profile 1.0; Debian 13 primary lane; Ubuntu 26.04 LTS comparison lane; POSIX.1-2024; cgroup v2; TLS 1.3; no containers or Kubernetes.
languageStrategy: Shell and Python for mechanisms and evidence; native Linux configuration for service, network, storage, and security boundaries.

modules.title: Processes, System Calls, Files, and Signals
modules.centralQuestion: How does a Linux process actually acquire resources, communicate, fail, and terminate?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Run the Atlas API and worker as separate processes with explicit descriptors, exit behavior, signal handling, and observable process ownership.
learningOutcomes: Trace a program from executable image through process creation, system calls, descriptors, and exit status.
Use `/proc`, `ps`, `lsof`, `strace`, and shell job control to explain observed behavior.
Distinguish process identity, parentage, sessions, process groups, and terminal ownership.
Design graceful `SIGTERM` handling without pretending `SIGKILL` can be handled.
Recognize descriptor leaks, zombie processes, orphaned children, and ambiguous shutdown.
Prove process behavior with transcripts and state observations rather than screenshots alone.

modules.title: Identity, Permissions, Capabilities, and Service Supervision
modules.centralQuestion: Which authority should each process possess, and who is responsible for keeping it running?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Give Atlas dedicated service identities, owned directories, restrictive modes, hardened systemd units, and unambiguous restart and shutdown policy.
learningOutcomes: Reason about users, groups, mode bits, umask, ACLs, set-user-ID, and effective identity.
Use Linux capabilities only when a narrow kernel privilege is genuinely required.
Separate code, configuration, mutable state, secrets, logs, and runtime files by ownership and lifecycle.
Design systemd service dependencies, restart policy, readiness, and sandboxing deliberately.
Reject root execution, writable code, and credential exposure as convenience shortcuts.
Verify unit syntax and the effective authority of a running process.

modules.title: CPU, Memory, Scheduling, Namespaces, and cgroups
modules.centralQuestion: How does the kernel share finite host resources, and how can one workload be bounded without making false isolation claims?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Publish and exercise a resource envelope for Atlas using cgroup v2 and systemd resource controls, with explicit throttling and memory-failure behavior.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish CPU time, load average, utilization, run-queue pressure, and throttling.
Explain virtual memory, resident memory, page cache, swap, overcommit, and out-of-memory selection.
Read cgroup v2 hierarchy, controller, and pressure evidence.
Use namespaces and cgroups as mechanisms without calling them complete security boundaries.
Choose CPU, memory, task, and file-descriptor limits from workload evidence.
Demonstrate bounded failure and recovery with safe stress fixtures.

modules.title: Storage, Filesystems, I/O, and Durability
modules.centralQuestion: When an application says that data was written, which bytes are actually durable and on which failure boundary?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Separate Atlas runtime, configuration, logs, queue state, and results; publish files atomically; and prove disk-full and restart behavior.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish files, directory entries, inodes, file descriptors, mounts, filesystems, and block devices.
Explain page cache, writeback, sync, fsync, rename, and directory durability.
Classify data as immutable code, configuration, ephemeral runtime state, logs, or durable application state.
Design atomic publication that does not cross filesystem boundaries.
Handle `ENOSPC`, inode exhaustion, partial writes, and interrupted cleanup explicitly.
Perform and verify a small backup-and-restore exercise rather than equating backup creation with recoverability.

modules.title: IP, Routing, Transport, and Sockets
modules.centralQuestion: How does a byte leave one process and reach the intended process across interfaces, routes, and transport state?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Define Atlas listening addresses, route assumptions, port ownership, timeouts, and dual-stack behavior; prove them with socket and packet-path evidence.
learningOutcomes: Read addresses, prefixes, interfaces, routes, and neighbor state for IPv4 and IPv6.
Trace a TCP connection through SYN, established state, shutdown, and TIME_WAIT.
Distinguish TCP streams, UDP datagrams, Unix-domain sockets, and their failure models.
Choose loopback, wildcard, private, and public bindings deliberately.
Use connect, read, write, and idle timeouts as separate controls.
Diagnose listening, routing, reachability, and application failures without guessing.

modules.title: DNS, HTTP, TLS, and PKI
modules.centralQuestion: How does a client turn a name into an authenticated application connection, and where can that chain fail?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Serve Atlas through an HTTPS edge with a local trust chain, correct names, certificate verification, rotation evidence, and protocol-aware health checks.
learningOutcomes: Explain recursive resolution, authoritative data, caching, TTLs, and negative answers.
Separate HTTP semantics from a particular transport version.
Trace TLS negotiation, certificate path validation, hostname verification, SNI, and ALPN.
Create and inspect a local CA and leaf certificate without normalizing insecure trust bypasses.
Distinguish encryption, server authentication, client authentication, and application authorization.
Diagnose name, trust, expiry, and protocol mismatch failures from evidence.

modules.title: Firewalls, NAT, Proxies, and Load Balancing
modules.centralQuestion: Which intermediary is allowed to accept, transform, route, or reject traffic, and which identity survives each hop?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Place Atlas behind a bounded reverse proxy, define host firewall policy, remove untrusted forwarding headers, and demonstrate health-aware backend removal.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish packet filtering, connection tracking, NAT, forwarding, proxying, and application routing.
Read a least-privilege nftables policy and predict its stateful behavior.
Separate forward proxies, reverse proxies, L4 load balancers, and L7 gateways.
Handle client identity and forwarding headers only across trusted proxy hops.
Design health checks, connection draining, and bounded retries without request amplification.
Explain what a load balancer can and cannot prove about application correctness.

modules.title: Virtualization, Images, Boot, and Cloud Compute
modules.centralQuestion: What changes—and what does not—when the Linux host becomes a virtual machine created from an image?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Define the Atlas machine image, boot sequence, cloud-init inputs, ephemeral-disk policy, metadata access, maintenance behavior, and replacement strategy.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish hardware virtualization, emulation, paravirtual devices, and process isolation.
Trace firmware, bootloader, kernel, initramfs, system manager, and service startup.
Separate immutable image content from instance configuration and mutable application data.
Use cloud-init and instance metadata without placing long-lived secrets in user data.
Treat instances as replaceable while preserving state according to explicit durability boundaries.
Model host maintenance, stop/start, reboot, termination, and image replacement as distinct events.

modules.title: Cloud Primitives, Identity, and Failure Domains
modules.centralQuestion: Which cloud resources and trust boundaries are required to preserve the host guarantees without copying one provider’s vocabulary into the architecture?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Publish provider-neutral compute, identity, network, storage, DNS, load-balancing, metadata, quota, and failure-domain requirements for Course 2.
learningOutcomes: Use the NIST cloud characteristics and service models without reducing cloud to “someone else’s server.”
Map regions, zones, virtual networks, subnets, routes, security controls, and managed services across providers.
Use workload identity and metadata services without storing static cloud keys on the host.
Separate block, object, and ephemeral storage guarantees.
Reason about quotas, control-plane APIs, eventual observation, cost, and shared responsibility.
Reject single-zone and single-instance designs that claim unsupported availability.

modules.title: Production Host Engineering and Final Defense
modules.centralQuestion: Can the host be installed, started, observed, upgraded, degraded, recovered, and replaced without making a claim stronger than the evidence?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Release Atlas Host Runtime 1.0, run a bounded failure game day, verify recovery, and export an exact Course 2 cloud-foundation requirements package.
learningOutcomes: Integrate service identity, resources, storage, network, TLS, firewall, supervision, logging, backup, and recovery into one host release.
Distinguish liveness, readiness, diagnostics, and business correctness.
Design patching, configuration change, rollback, certificate rotation, and machine replacement procedures.
Use structured evidence and runbooks during a multi-fault exercise.
Classify local, Linux-privileged, VM, and real-cloud evidence honestly.
Defend every outgoing infrastructure requirement and its failure assumption.
